content.title: About
content.content: Pumpkin, canned, cooked is a ready‑to‑eat product made from ripe pumpkin that is peeled, diced, boiled until tender, and then sealed in glass or metal jars with a small amount of salt and water.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pumpkin is rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Canning preserves pumpkin nutrients for up to 2‑3 years when stored properly.
Pumpkin is a traditional ingredient in many cuisines, from American pumpkin pie to Indian curries.
Canned pumpkin retains its natural sweetness and a faint nutty note.
Pumpkin belongs to the Cucurbitaceae family, which also includes zucchini, cucumber, and watermelon.

items.title: High in vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Pumpkin is low in calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports heart function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Compounds such as vitamin C and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Pumpkin allergy
items.content: Although rare, pumpkin allergy can cause skin reactions or gastrointestinal upset.

items.title: Bacterial contamination if improperly stored
items.content: Bulging or damaged cans may harbor pathogens and should be discarded.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add pumpkin to soups, stews, pasta sauces, salads, or use it as a filling for pies. It can be quickly reheated in the microwave and served as a side dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct light. Once opened, refrigerate and consume within 3‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Sesame dressing is a flavorful sauce made from ground sesame seeds (tahini), soy sauce, rice vinegar, honey or sugar, and vegetable oil. It has a rich nutty taste, subtle sweetness and a gentle tang, making it popular in Asian cuisine, especially in salads, marinades and noodle dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sesame is one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown for more than 5,000 years.
Tahini, a paste of ground sesame, forms the base of most sesame dressing recipes.
Sesame dressing is commonly used in Japanese goma‑a‑o salad and Korean bibimbap.
Sesame seeds contain lignans that give the dressing its characteristic golden‑brown color.
In traditional Chinese medicine, sesame is considered a warming, tonic food.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: Sesame provides monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of calcium and magnesium
items.content: The dressing supplies important minerals that contribute to bone strength and normal muscle function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lignans and vitamin E in sesame help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Sesame seeds are high in dietary fiber, which promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Provides plant protein
items.content: While not a major protein source, the dressing adds a modest amount of plant‑based protein, useful in vegetarian diets.

items.title: Sesame allergy
items.content: Sesame is one of the top eight food allergens; reactions can be severe.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce adds significant salt, so people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of oil and sweeteners, the dressing is relatively calorie‑dense; moderation is key for weight management.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some recipes include honey or sugar, which may be unsuitable for individuals with diabetes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sesame dressing is perfect for dressing salads, marinating fish, chicken or tofu, and as a sauce for noodles, rice dishes and sushi rolls. It can also be stirred into soups or used as a dip for vegetables and crackers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dressing in a tightly sealed jar in the refrigerator. When kept properly, it retains its flavor for 1–2 months. Discard if you notice off‑odors, color changes, or mold.

shellfish-mixture-and-vegetables-excludi.title: Shellfish mixture and vegetables without carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens, potatoes, or soy sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The shellfish mixture with vegetables is a ready‑to‑cook blend of shrimp, squid, mussels and selected vegetables such as sweet pepper, zucchini, cauliflower and onion. It does not contain carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens, potatoes or soy‑based sauce, making it suitable for those avoiding these ingredients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shellfish are rich in omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart and brain health.
The blend is prepared without soy sauce, reducing glutamate content for people sensitive to soy.
Included vegetables cook quickly by steaming or sautéing, preserving most of their vitamins.
Traditionally used in Asian cuisine, this mix is now popular in health‑focused meals worldwide.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Shellfish provide complete animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA from the seafood help reduce inflammation and support cardiovascular function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The mix supplies B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It contains zinc, selenium and iodine, which aid immune function and thyroid health.

items.title: Low carbohydrate content
items.content: Absence of potatoes and starchy vegetables makes it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels or squid.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shellfish contain cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Food interactions
items.content: Omega‑3 can enhance the effect of blood thinners; consult a healthcare professional if you take such medication.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Quickly stir‑fry the mix in olive oil, steam it, or add it to soups and rice dishes. Serve with lemon, fresh herbs (parsley, dill) and a drizzle of olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months. Discard if any off‑smell or signs of spoilage appear.

content.title: About
content.content: Meatball soup is a classic Russian dish consisting of a flavorful broth with small meatballs. Made from beef or pork, onion, carrot, potato and spices, it combines nourishment with a comforting taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the 19th century and quickly became a staple in working‑class families.
Meatballs are usually a mixture of beef and pork, sometimes enriched with rice or semolina for a softer texture.
Traditional recipes include a bay leaf and whole black peppercorns.
The soup is often served with sour cream and fresh herbs.
During the Soviet era it was a common first course in school cafeterias.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Meatballs provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef and pork contain heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The soup supplies vitamins B12 and B6, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Vegetable nutrients
items.content: Potato, carrot and onion add fiber, vitamin C and potassium.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A warm broth helps maintain fluid balance, especially in cold weather.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Using ready‑made broth cubes can raise salt levels; adjust seasoning accordingly.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rare individuals allergic to beef or pork may experience reactions.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Fat depends on the cut of meat; choose lean cuts or trim excess fat.

items.title: Thorough cooking
items.content: Meatballs must be fully cooked to eliminate the risk of food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often topped with a dollop of sour cream, fresh dill or parsley, and a slice of rye bread. Meatballs can be gently mashed with a fork for a softer bite.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat until boiling to ensure safety.

spinach-fresh-cooked-with-butter-or-marg.title: Spinach, fresh, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a leafy vegetable rich in vitamins and minerals. When cooked with butter or margarine, it retains a delicate flavor and gains additional fat‑soluble benefits.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach is famous for its high iron content, but iron absorption improves when paired with fat.
The old culinary term “spinach” often refers to dishes where the leaves are sautéed in butter.
In ancient Rome, spinach was considered a “food of the gods” because of its vivid green color.
There are more than 20 spinach varieties, differing in leaf thickness and taste.
Spinach is a staple in many world cuisines: Italian pasta with spinach, French épinards à la crème, Indian palak paneer.

items.title: Rich in vitamins A, C, K
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, vitamin C boosts immunity, and vitamin K is essential for blood clotting.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during periods of rapid growth, such as pregnancy.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium and magnesium help maintain normal blood pressure, while plant fiber can lower cholesterol.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Fiber promotes intestinal motility and supports the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to spinach.

items.title: Nitrate content
items.content: Intensively fertilized crops can have higher nitrate levels; always wash the leaves thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté spinach in butter or margarine for 2‑3 minutes until wilted. Add a pinch of salt, garlic, or lemon juice for flavor. Serve as a side dish, in omelets, pasta, or casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh spinach in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or container covered with a damp towel, for up to 3‑5 days. Cooked spinach should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 2 days.
